content.content:
## How We Sound -- and Why It Matters

Every single person who speaks English has an accent. There is no such thing as "accent-free" English -- even the most "neutral" General American or RP speaker has an accent that can be identified and analysed. Your accent quietly broadcasts where you are from, what languages you speak, and often which social group you belong to. It is one of the most immediate markers of identity there is.

But accents are not just neutral facts. They carry social weight. Some accents are heard as "educated" or "professional," while others are stigmatised or mocked. To understand English as a global language, you need to understand both how pronunciation works and how society reacts to different ways of speaking. In this chapter we will cover the basics of phonetics, the difference between accent and dialect, why some accents carry more prestige than others, and how accent discrimination harms real people -- including how your own Norwegian-accented English fits into the picture.

## The Building Blocks of Sound

**Phonetics** is the study of the physical sounds of speech, and understanding a few basics helps you analyse accents and improve your own pronunciation.

**Vowels** are made with an open vocal tract, and English has far more of them than most languages -- the five vowel letters represent around twenty different vowel sounds, which is a big reason English spelling is so irregular. Key distinctions include short versus long ("ship" /ɪ/ versus "sheep" /iː/) and monophthongs versus diphthongs ("go" glides from one position to another). The most common vowel sound of all is the **schwa** /ə/, the relaxed sound in unstressed syllables like "about" or "banana."

**Consonants** are made by obstructing airflow. English has some globally rare sounds, especially the two "th" sounds /θ/ and /ð/, which many accents replace with /t/, /d/, /s/, or /f/. The /r/ is pronounced very differently across accents -- retroflex in American, an approximant in RP, tapped in Scottish.

Beyond individual sounds, **stress and rhythm** shape how an accent feels. English is **stress-timed**: stressed syllables fall at roughly regular intervals while unstressed ones get squeezed. Many other languages, including French, Spanish, and Hindi, are **syllable-timed**, giving each syllable equal time -- which is one of the most noticeable features of a non-native accent. Finally, **intonation** carries meaning too: rising intonation at the end usually signals a question, falling intonation a statement, and the spreading "uptalk" (rising intonation on statements) is associated with Australian and Californian English. Take a single word like "water": it becomes /ˈwɔːtə/ in RP, /ˈwɑːɾɚ/ in General American, /ˈwoʔə/ in Cockney, and a retroflex form in Indian English -- all communicating exactly the same meaning.

options.text: placeholder
A rare consonant found only in Scottish
The most common English vowel sound, found in unstressed syllables like 'about'
A type of rising intonation
The /r/ sound in American English

questions.solution: The schwa /ə/ is the relaxed, central vowel of unstressed syllables (about, banana, the). It is the most common vowel sound in English.

questions.task: What does it mean that English is 'stress-timed'?

options.text: Every syllable takes exactly the same time
There is no stress at all
Stressed syllables occur at regular intervals while unstressed ones are compressed
Only the last syllable is ever stressed

questions.solution: English is stress-timed: stressed syllables come at roughly regular intervals and unstressed syllables get squeezed. Many other languages are syllable-timed, giving each syllable equal time.

questions.task: Why is English spelling so irregular when it comes to vowels?

options.text: English has no vowels at all
Every word is spelled phonetically
Vowels are never written down
The five vowel letters must represent about twenty different vowel sounds

questions.solution: English has roughly twenty vowel sounds but only five vowel letters, which is a major reason its spelling is irregular.

questions.task: What do the five accents pronouncing 'water' differently have in common?

options.text: They all communicate exactly the same meaning
They all sound identical
Only one is grammatically correct
They reflect different intelligence levels

questions.solution: Different pronunciations of 'water' across accents are systematic and predictable, reflecting the speaker's linguistic background -- not their intelligence or education. All convey the same meaning.

content.content:
## Prestige, Discrimination, and Your Accent

Some accents carry **prestige** -- they are socially valued and associated with education, authority, and competence. In the English-speaking world, the main prestige accents are RP in Britain (though its prestige is fading) and General American in the USA and internationally. But here is the crucial point: prestige is a *social* phenomenon, not a linguistic one. No accent is inherently "better," "clearer," or "more correct" than any other. The prestige of an accent simply reflects the power and status of the people who speak it.

This matters because of **accent discrimination**, or accentism -- judging, stereotyping, or treating people unfairly based on how they speak. It is a serious and well-documented problem. Studies show people associate certain accents with intelligence and competence even with no rational basis: Birmingham (Brummie) accents are consistently rated as less intelligent despite no evidence, and Southern American accents are stereotyped as "slow." Non-native accents can lead to discrimination in job interviews, housing, and customer service, and "linguistic profiling" -- judging someone's race or ethnicity by their voice -- has been documented in housing studies.

Accent is also tied to identity. People often modify their accent in different situations (a process called **accommodation**), and **code-switching** between a professional accent at work and a regional accent at home is common and mentally demanding. Losing or changing your accent can feel like losing part of yourself, and the pressure to adopt a prestige accent can act as a form of social control. For you as a Norwegian speaker, the takeaway is reassuring: you will always have a Norwegian accent in English, and that is perfectly fine. Your accent is part of your identity. The goal is mutual intelligibility, not sounding like a native speaker.

options.text: placeholder

questions.task: Where does the prestige of an accent like RP come from?

options.text: The fact that it is objectively clearer than other accents
The social power and status of its speakers, not any linguistic superiority
Its perfect grammar
Its greater number of vowels

questions.solution: Prestige is a social phenomenon. No accent is inherently better or clearer; prestige reflects the power and status of the people who speak it.

options.text: Teaching everyone the same accent
Studying the history of accents
Judging or treating people unfairly based on how they speak
Pronouncing words very slowly

questions.solution: Accentism is judging, stereotyping, or mistreating people based on their accent. It is well-documented in employment, housing, and customer service.

questions.task: What does the chapter advise Norwegian speakers about their accent in English?

options.text: They must eliminate their accent to be understood
They should only speak RP
They should avoid speaking English entirely
A Norwegian accent is fine -- the goal is mutual intelligibility, not native-like sound

questions.solution: The chapter reassures Norwegian speakers that their accent is part of their identity and perfectly acceptable. The aim is to be understood, not to imitate a native speaker.

questions.task: What is 'accommodation' in relation to accent?

options.text: Adjusting your accent or speech to fit different social situations
Refusing to ever change how you speak
Speaking only your home dialect everywhere
Mocking other people's accents

questions.solution: Accommodation is adjusting your speech -- including your accent -- to different situations, such as using a professional accent at work and a regional one at home.

## Summary

Pronunciation shapes how we are perceived and how we perceive others. Every English speaker has an accent, and no accent is inherently superior. The basics of **phonetics** -- vowels (including the all-important schwa), consonants (like the globally rare "th" sounds), stress-timed versus syllable-timed **rhythm**, and **intonation** -- help us analyse how accents differ. **Prestige accents** like RP and General American derive their status from social power, not linguistic quality, and **accent discrimination** is a real, harmful phenomenon affecting people's opportunities in work, housing, and daily life. As speakers of English in a global context, the goal is mutual intelligibility, not imitation -- which is why your own Norwegian-accented English is entirely valid and a natural part of your identity.
